alertExcerpt:
- alert: ServiceInstanceDown
        expr: up{job=~".*-service"} == 0
        for: 4s
        labels: {severity: critical}
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.instance }} is not responding to metric scrapes"
          response: "Gateway ejects the instance; restart policy restarts the container. Page on-call if > 60s."

      - alert: InstanceRestarted
        expr: changes(process_start_time_seconds{job=~".*-service"}[1m]) > 0
        for: 0s
        labels: {severity: info}
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.instance }} restarted (crash masked by self-healing)"
          response: "No user impact expected; find the crash cause in the logs. Repeated restarts = crash loop."

      - alert: DatabasePrimaryDown
        expr: max(dependency_up{dependency="db_primary"}) == 0
        for: 4s
        labels: {severity: critical}
        annotations:
          summary: "No service can reach the primary PostgreSQL database"

notes.abstract: This report presents the endterm extension of a fault-tolerant university information system built from four Python/FastAPI microservices (student, payment, academic records, timetable), an nginx API gateway, PostgreSQL with a streaming replica and periodic backups, and a Prometheus/Grafana monitoring stack, all deployed with Docker Compose. A midterm-scope baseline configuration (single instances, no timeouts, retries, idempotency or authentication) is kept and compared with the resilient endterm configuration, which adds replication, automatic recovery, timeouts, bounded retries, circuit breakers, idempotent atomic payments, read failover, graceful degradation, request-ID correlation, alerting and a set of security controls. Ten repeatable experiments with 38 measured runs inject instance and node crashes, a hanging dependency, a database crash, a 15x load spike, monitoring incidents, unauthorized access, malformed and abusive requests, and crashes inside payment transactions. After an instance crash the share of successful requests rose from 52.8% (baseline) to 100%, and recovery time fell from 21.0 s to 1.9 s; during a database crash from 34.3% to 100%; under a hanging dependency the baseline suffered a cascading failure while the resilient system degraded gracefully with no collateral failures. All 10 unauthorized-access cases succeeded against the baseline and all 10 were denied and audited by the resilient system. Retried payments created 34 duplicate charges in the baseline and none in the resilient system. All alerts fired within 9-15 s without false positives. The modelled availability rises from 99.87% (baseline with manual repair) to 99.9996%. Limitations, including the single-host setup and the load-generator capacity, are discussed.
notes.overview: The resilient configuration masked every infrastructure fault that has redundancy: instance crash, node loss, database crash and random crashes (E1, E2, E4, E10) produced zero failed requests over 10 runs and about 17,000 requests, compared with 34-84% success after the fault in the baseline. The only fault it could not fully mask is the hanging timetable service (E3), which deliberately has a single instance; there the resilient system contained the fault (no collateral damage, dashboards degraded) instead of masking it. In the load spike (E5) both configurations stayed at 100% success, so the comparison there shows the cost of the extra controls rather than a resilience gain.
notes.E1_limit: Crash is a clean SIGKILL; the baseline recovery uses an optimistic simulated operator (10 s reaction). The ServiceInstanceDown alert cannot see crashes shorter than its 4 s window (see InstanceRestarted).
notes.E1: In the baseline the crashed container disappears from the network, so nginx keeps waiting for a connection (default 60 s) and clients see 5 s timeouts rather than fast errors: about 496 failed requests per run, 20.4 s of user-visible impact, and recovery only after the simulated operator restarted the service (21.0 s after the fault; the alert itself fired after 8.8 s). Because student-service also authenticates users and feeds the dashboard and transcript, its loss affected almost every operation. In the resilient configuration the gateway retried idempotent requests on student-2 and ejected student-1, the restart policy brought the process back in 1.9 s, and none of the 4,047 requests in three runs failed (p95 16 ms). ServiceInstanceDown did not fire because the outage was shorter than its 4 s window; that is correct for paging, but it means a masked crash was invisible to the team, which led to the InstanceRestarted alert (Section 4.4).
notes.E2: Losing three containers at once had almost the same effect on the baseline as E1 (54.4% success after the fault, 21.2 s impact), because each of the lost containers was the only instance of its service. The resilient system served all 4,497 requests of three runs; the p95 rose slightly (24 ms, maximum 37 ms) because the first requests to the vanished node waited for the 1 s connect timeout before nginx failed over and ejected it. ServiceInstanceDown fired for all three instances after 8.5 s, i.e. the sustained outage was detected while users saw no impact, and the node came back 2.9 s after the repair at t = 30 s.
notes.E3: This experiment shows why timeouts matter more than redundancy for some faults. In the baseline the dashboard calls the frozen timetable service without a timeout, so every dashboard request blocks a worker thread; after a few seconds all 40 threads of student-service were blocked and even requests that do not use the timetable failed: 149 of about 247 profile and transcript requests per run (transcripts call student-service internally). Success dropped to 0% for 12 s (Figure). In the resilient system each timetable call is cut off after 0.8 s; after three consecutive timeouts the circuit breaker opens and later dashboards skip the dependency immediately and return the profile and balance with `degraded: ["timetable"]` (311 degraded responses per run, dashboard p95 812 ms during the fault, CircuitBreakerOpen alert after 6.4 s). No unrelated request failed. The 90 failed requests per run are direct calls to the frozen timetable endpoint, which the gateway ends after its 5 s read timeout; they could be shortened with a tighter timeout or served from a cache, which is listed as future work.
notes.E4: A database crash is the most damaging fault for the baseline: 34.3% success after the fault on average, with a large spread (7.3-48.1%). After the operator restarted PostgreSQL (27.9 s), the baseline services still held broken pooled connections because the pool does not validate them, so errors continued; in the first repetition the service had not recovered by the end of the run (impact 50.5 s). Detection took 14.8 s (2 s probe + 4 s alert window + scrape and evaluation). In the resilient system the restart policy restarted PostgreSQL, which completed crash recovery in 1.3 s; during that time reads were served by the replica (45 degraded responses per run marked `read_from_replica`), validated pools discarded the broken connections, and none of the 4,947 requests failed, including all writes. No payment was lost or half-applied in either configuration in this experiment.
notes.E5: At 300 requests/s neither configuration was saturated: both served 100% of the requests. The resilient configuration was slightly slower (p95 15-21 ms vs 12.5 ms) because every request is authenticated (JWT verification), every pooled connection is validated before use, writes are audited, the gateway applies rate limiting, and each container is capped at one CPU. This 3-8 ms is the measured price of the controls. The experiment therefore confirms requirement R5 for the resilient system but cannot show a capacity advantage, because the generators (not the system) were the limit.
notes.E6: All three injected incidents raised the expected alert: HighLatencyP95 after 12.6 s, HighErrorRate after 15.0 s and AuthFailureSpike after 9.3 s, and each resolved after the fault was removed. No other alert fired. The delays are dominated by the 20 s rate window plus the 6 s `for` duration; they can be shortened at the cost of more false positives. In the first pass AuthFailureSpike did not fire, because the failure counter series only appeared with the first failed login and Prometheus' rate() ignores the jump from a missing series; pre-creating the series fixed it.
notes.E7: The baseline has no authentication, so all ten attacks succeeded: anybody could read any student's profile and transcript, read the audit log, change a grade (the grade checksum changed) and create a payment for another student, without leaving any audit record. In the resilient system all ten were denied with the correct status (401 for missing, forged, expired and alg=none tokens; 403 for IDOR and role violations; 404 for the hidden internal route), nothing was exposed or changed, and nine denials were written to the audit log with actor, path, reason and request ID. The tenth (internal route) is stopped by the gateway before it reaches a service and appears in the gateway access log.
notes.E8: The baseline only rejected the two requests that FastAPI's type checking catches. It stored five invalid payments (negative amount, unknown method, a script tag and an SQL fragment as the term, a 64 KB term) and an invalid grade, and two inputs caused server errors (an amount that overflows the numeric column returned 500, and the request with a script tag in the term ended with 502 Bad Gateway). SQL injection did not execute in either configuration because all queries are parameterized, but the baseline stored the payload as data. The resilient system rejected all ten requests (nine with 422 from validation, one with 413 from the gateway body limit), stored nothing invalid and produced no 5xx. A single client sending 400 requests in about 2 s got 148 served and 252 throttled with 429, while another user's 40 requests at the same time all succeeded (p95 18.5 ms). Of 100 password guesses, 62 were evaluated and 38 throttled; all containers stayed healthy.
notes.E9: This is the most important result for a payment system. When 30% of committed payments lost their response, the client retried with the same key and the baseline charged again each time: 134 rows for 100 payments, 34 duplicates, and students were charged 3,350.00 instead of 2,500.00. The resilient system recognized each retry by its Idempotency-Key and returned the original payment: 100 rows, no duplicates, totals equal. When the process was killed between the payment insert and the balance update, the baseline (autocommit) left a payment row without its balance update (one account mismatch) and also produced three duplicates. In the resilient system the whole transaction rolled back on every crash: no duplicates, no lost payments, no mismatches. 22 of the 80 resilient payments were not acknowledged because at times both payment instances were restarting and the client's retry budget (about 1.4 s) was shorter than the restart; those payments were not charged either, so the client can safely retry them later with the same key. The resilient system chooses consistency over availability for writes, which is the correct trade-off for money.
notes.E10: Over three minutes of random crashes the baseline lost about 20.8 s of service per crash and served 87.3% of all requests (83.6% after the first crash). The resilient system served all 3,599 requests; its restarts were faster than the probe could observe across seven containers.
notes.reliability: Two conclusions follow. First, replication changes the order of magnitude: with two replicas the unavailability of a critical service falls from 8.1e-6 (one instance, 21 s MTTR) or 3.5e-4 (realistic 15-minute manual repair) to about 5e-13, so service instances stop contributing to downtime. Second, what remains is dominated by components that are still single: the gateway and the database primary for writes. The resilient total of 99.9996% (about 2.1 min/year) meets requirement R10 (>= 99.95%); the baseline meets it only with the unrealistic 10-second operator (99.9934%) and misses it clearly with manual repair (99.87%, about 11.4 hours/year). The model assumes independent failures and perfect failover. E3 shows a dependent failure (a slow dependency taking down healthy services) that a series/parallel model cannot capture; timeouts and circuit breakers are what make the independence assumption hold. The soak test's observed failure rate (40-60 per hour) is deliberately far higher than the assumed MTTF of 720 h, so the soak availability (87.3% vs 100%) is a stress result, not an estimate of production availability.

discussion: The experiments support the success criterion of the assignment: the extended system detected the selected incidents, limited the impact of service failures and tested misuse, recovered predictably and preserved data integrity, and every claim is backed by a measured run against the baseline. Three observations stand out.

First, redundancy alone is not enough. Replicas masked crashes (E1, E2, E10), but the most dramatic baseline failure, E3, was caused by a slow dependency, and replicas would not have helped there: every replica would have blocked in the same way. Timeouts, circuit breakers and graceful degradation are what turned a platform-wide outage into a partial, clearly reported degradation. Likewise, fast failure is better than slow failure: the baseline's failures were 5 s timeouts, which hold resources and frustrate users far more than an immediate 503.

Second, correctness under failure needs explicit design. Retrying is necessary for availability but is exactly what produced 34 duplicate charges in the baseline (E9). Idempotency keys and atomic transactions made retries safe; without them, the resilience mechanisms would have made data integrity worse. The same is true of read failover: the replica can serve reads, but writes are refused rather than diverging, a deliberate consistency-over-availability choice.

Third, observability needs validation like any other feature. Two monitoring defects were found only because the alerts were tested: masked crashes produced no alert (fixed with InstanceRestarted) and a lazily created counter hid the first burst of authentication failures (fixed by pre-creating series). Request IDs made diagnosis fast: one ID retrieves the gateway entry, the services involved, the upstream instance and any retries or degradations.

The controls have a measurable cost: about 3-8 ms of extra p95 latency at 300 requests/s (E5), more containers and more configuration. For a university system that handles money and personal data this cost is clearly acceptable, but it should be measured, not assumed, as was done here.
limitations: Single physical host: "nodes" are groups of containers, so network partitions, disk failures and correlated host failures were not tested. RAID and ECC are documented, not demonstrated.
The gateway and the database primary (for writes) remain single points of failure; there is no automatic replica promotion.
The baseline recovery uses a simulated operator with a 10 s reaction time, which flatters the baseline; a realistic manual MTTR is only modelled (Section 8.12).
Load-generator capacity limited the spike to 300 requests/s, below the saturation point of both configurations; the generators share the host with the system.
MTTF values are assumptions; only MTTR values are measured. The number of repetitions (1-3) is small, so the ranges are indicative rather than statistically rigorous.
Logs are collected with docker logs rather than a central log store (e.g. Loki/ELK); tracing uses request IDs, not a full distributed-tracing system such as OpenTelemetry.
Another unrelated Docker project was running on the same host during the measurements; both configurations were measured under the same conditions.
Fault injection uses a test-only /chaos endpoint; it is disabled unless CHAOS_ENABLED is set and is not routed by the gateway, but it would have to be removed from production images.
lessons: Measure the harness before measuring the system: the first load-spike results were caused by the Windows port-forwarding path, not by the services. A control run against a static endpoint exposed this.
Test the alerts with injected incidents; two monitoring defects would otherwise have gone unnoticed.
Retries must come with idempotency, and every retry layer needs a budget shorter than the timeout of the caller above it.
Pool validation (check on checkout) is a small setting with a large effect: without it the baseline kept failing long after the database was back.
Keeping a baseline in the same code base, selected by one variable, made the comparison fair and cheap to repeat.
conclusion: The project extended a midterm-scope university information system into a cloud-ready microservice platform with resilience, observability and security controls, and evaluated it with ten repeatable experiments against the retained baseline. With replicas, automatic restart and gateway failover, crashes of instances, nodes and the database were masked completely (100% success, recovery in about 1-2 s instead of 21-28 s with an operator). Timeouts and circuit breakers prevented a hanging dependency from cascading. Idempotency keys and atomic transactions eliminated the duplicate and partially applied payments that the baseline produced. Authentication, authorization, validation and rate limiting stopped every tested attack and malformed request and left an audit trail, and the alert rules detected every injected incident within 15 s without false positives.

The remaining risks are known and documented: the single gateway and write primary, the single-host test environment, and the capacity of the load generator. The next steps would be a second gateway behind a virtual IP or cloud load balancer, automatic database failover (Patroni or a managed service), a Kubernetes deployment across several nodes, centralized logs and OpenTelemetry tracing, and load tests from a dedicated machine.

E1_instance_crash.baseline: Correct: ServiceInstanceDown{student-1} after 8.8 s. records-1 and payment-1 were also reported down (their metrics endpoint hung while they waited for student-service without a timeout) and HighErrorRate/HighLatencyP95 fired for them: true symptoms of the cascade. No false positives.
E1_instance_crash.resilient: No alert: the crash was masked in 1.9 s, shorter than the 4 s window, so a harmless but real event went unnoticed (missed detection). Fixed afterwards with InstanceRestarted (validated: fired 5.4 s after a crash).

E2_node_failure.baseline: Correct: ServiceInstanceDown for the three node-A instances after 8.8 s.
E2_node_failure.resilient: Correct: the same three alerts after 8.5 s although users saw no errors, so the team learns about the lost node.

E3_dependency_timeout.baseline: Correct: ServiceInstanceDown{timetable-1} after 7.8 s; student-1 and records-1 were also reported down (thread exhaustion) and HighLatencyP95 fired: true symptoms of the cascade.
E3_dependency_timeout.resilient: Correct: ServiceInstanceDown{timetable-1} (9.1 s) and CircuitBreakerOpen{student -> timetable} (6.4 s); in one run also HighLatencyP95{student-service} for the 0.8 s degraded dashboards. No false positives.

E4_database_failure.baseline: Correct: DatabasePrimaryDown after 14.8 s, plus instance-down, error-rate and latency alerts on services that were really failing.
E4_database_failure.resilient: Detected indirectly: DatabasePrimaryDown did not fire (1.3 s outage < 4 s window), but CircuitBreakerOpen (db_primary or timetable) fired 6.5-8.5 s and HighLatencyP95 12.5-14.6 s after the crash in all runs. True positives.

E5_load_spike.baseline: Correct: no alerts (no incident; latency far below 500 ms).
E5_load_spike.resilient: Correct: no alerts (no incident; latency far below 500 ms).

E10_chaos_soak.baseline: Correct: one ServiceInstanceDown per crash plus error-rate and latency alerts during each outage.
E10_chaos_soak.resilient: No alerts: every crash was masked within about 2 s (InstanceRestarted was not deployed yet during this run).
